# LLM provider validation campaigns

This folder carries the **real-execution evidence** for Orkeon's 16 LLM providers (fourteen
vendors and two aggregators): the scripts that launch the campaigns, and the archived report
of each one.

> **Why this folder exists.** The repository holds ~400 unit tests on the LLM providers,
> and **every one of them talks to a mocked HTTP handler**. A mock proves that Orkeon sends
> what we think it sends; it does not prove that the provider accepts it. It is that second
> proof which is built here.
>
> **Protocol reference.** Modes M1–M14 and the campaign journal are defined by
> `LLM-PROVIDERS-TEST-MATRIX.md` (§5 and §7) and the chantier sheet `LLM-08`, two documents
> of the maintainers' internal tracking that are **not published** — hence the absence of a
> link. This file is self-sufficient: the modes are recalled below, and every report ends
> with the fragments ready to paste into the matrix. The matrix only consolidates, on the
> maintainers' side, what the reports in this folder already establish.

## Prerequisites

| | Linux / macOS (`run-campaign.sh`) | Windows (`run-campaign.ps1`) |
|---|---|---|
| **jq** | **required** — reads the campaign JSON and renders the report | no: PowerShell has `ConvertFrom-Json` |
| bash | ≥ 4 (`mapfile`, associative arrays) — macOS's bash 3.2 is not enough | ➖ |
| PowerShell | ➖ | ≥ 7 |
| .NET SDK | required, unless the `orkeon` tool is already installed or `ORKEON_BIN` is set | same |

```bash
# Debian / Ubuntu / WSL
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y jq
# macOS
brew install jq
```

The PowerShell mirror has **no external dependency** beyond .NET: on Windows,
`run-campaign.ps1` works without installing anything else.

## Getting started

```bash
# 1. Start from the template — never the other way round: providers.example.json is versioned.
cp llmproviders-test/providers.example.json llmproviders-test/providers.local.json

# 2. Fill in the environment variables that file names.
export OPENAI_API_KEY=…

# 3. See what would run, without spending a credit.
llmproviders-test/run-campaign.sh --all --config llmproviders-test/providers.local.json --dry-run

# 4. Run it for real — Ollama first, its cost is zero.
llmproviders-test/run-campaign.sh --provider ollama --model llama3.2
```

On Windows, `run-campaign.ps1` exposes exactly the same options.

## Options

| Option | Role |
|---|---|
| `--provider <keys>` | One key, or several separated by commas — `openai`, `anthropic`, `ollama`, `azure`, `together`, `qwen`, `deepseek`, `kimi`, `mistral`, `huggingface`, `zai`, `gemini`, `grok`, `minimax`, `openrouter`, `mammouth`; the decision providers `typesafe`, `liquid`, `kev` (modes D1–D8) |
| `--all` | Every provider declared in the JSON |
| `--parallel` | Runs the selected providers simultaneously (see below) |
| `--model <id\|glob>` | An identifier, or a pattern (`gpt-5.6-*`, `*flash*`) |
| `--modes M1,M8` | Default: the provider's own set from the catalog (`modes`: D1–D7 for a decision provider; the paid D8 only when named), else every chat mode of the harness |
| `--config <file>` | Campaign configuration (see `providers.schema.json`) |
| `--base-url <url>` | Endpoint override (Azure, regional mirrors) |
| `--api-version <v>` | Azure `api-version` in deployment mode |
| `--workspace-id <w>` | Workspace of the requests, for workspace-scoped keys — Anthropic's identity-linked keys require it (also declarable per provider: `workspaceId` in the JSON) |
| `--api-key-env <VAR>` | Variable carrying the key |
| `--max-models <n>` | Wildcard cap (default 5; `providers.example.json` lowers it to 3) |
| `--candidates` | After each provider's default, also runs the successors the catalog records as `candidateModels` (review of 2026-09-19), same modes — the campaign that can promote one of them to default. Automatic path only |
| `--dry-run` | Resolves and prints the plan, calls nothing |
| `--no-preflight` | Skips the one-call check that opens each provider (below) |
| `--no-recap` | Does not rebuild the index — for parallel launches |
| `--timeout <s>` | Per-request deadline, default **180 s** (a cold local model has to load first) |
| `--temperature <t>` | Sampling, default **0** — pinned so that a verdict is reproducible. Models that require another value are recorded **per model** in `requiredParams` (catalog) and resolved automatically |
| `--thinking-effort <e>` | Base reasoning effort (e.g. `none`) — for models that refuse tools while reasoning; recorded per model in `requiredParams` (catalog) |
| `--out <dir>` | Root of the reports (default: this folder) |

## Running several providers in parallel

Campaigns are long and independent. `--provider` accepts a list and `--parallel` runs them
together:

```bash
export DEEPSEEK_API_KEY=…  ZAI_API_KEY=…

llmproviders-test/run-campaign.sh --provider deepseek,zai,ollama --parallel
```

A single campaign, a single index rebuilt at the end, a single exit code. The key variables
are resolved per provider from the catalog, so a heterogeneous list needs no `-k` at all.

**What is parallelised, and what is not.** Providers run side by side; the models of the
*same* provider stay serial. They share its quota, and running them together would measure
the throttling rather than the protocol.

**The output stays readable.** Each provider writes into its own buffer, replayed at the end
in the order you named them — a parallel run reads exactly like a sequential one. The price
is that there is no fine-grained live progress: only the `▶ … — started` lines arrive
immediately.

**If a process dies** without reporting back, it is counted as a failure. A crash that passed
for a success would be worse than a red.

### What the script checks around the runs

**A preflight opens each provider.** Before its models run, one call of the provider's first
mode (M1, or D1 for a decision provider) goes to its first model. A refused key, an empty
balance or an exhausted quota (`401`, `402`, `403`, `insufficient_balance`, Z.AI's `1113`,
Kimi's `exceeded_current_quota_error`) skips the provider there, and the closing line counts
it apart from the failed modes. Any other red lets the campaign run: a model-level red is a
finding. On 2026-11-11 an empty Z.AI balance failed every mode of five models one after the
other, each 429 retried as a rate limit — 21 minutes for nothing; the preflight turns that
into one call. `--no-preflight` skips it. Since issue #328 that 429 is no longer retried:
the preflight answers on its first call.

**The commit names the code that ran.** The reports carry the short commit of `HEAD`, with
`-dirty` when `src/` holds uncommitted changes: the commit alone would then name code that
did not run.

**The catalogue is compared with the snapshot.** After a provider's runs, its live listing
(`orkeon llm models`, free) is compared with `lib/served-models.json`; the identifiers it
serves that the snapshot does not list, and those it no longer serves, are printed at the
end of the campaign. A new identifier is a candidate; a withdrawn one may be a default.

**A report points at the notes, it does not copy them.** The provider's points of attention
live in `lib/catalog.json` (`notes`) and change from one campaign to the next; a copy in each
report went stale at the next one. The report names where they are kept.

To launch several separate *processes* — several terminals, a scheduler — the precaution
remains to **defer the index** with `--no-recap`, then rebuild it once:

```bash
llmproviders-test/run-campaign.sh --provider deepseek --no-recap &
llmproviders-test/run-campaign.sh --provider zai      --no-recap &
wait
llmproviders-test/lib/recap.sh llmproviders-test
```

Without this, two campaigns finishing together each rebuild the recap from a snapshot taken
before the other had dropped its report, and the last one to write produces a complete but
stale index. The write is atomic (temporary file then rename), so forgetting it corrupts
nothing: it can only leave the index one line behind, which the next rebuild catches up.

## API keys

**Never as a command-line argument** — the harness refuses it, and the kit does not work
around it. A key arrives through an environment variable, or through the `apiKey` field of a
configuration file that the scripts **refuse to read** unless it is named `*.local.json` or
`*.secrets.json`. Both patterns are gitignored.

The generated reports are versioned: they are the "archived output" that LLM-08 requires as
its level of evidence. They are built from the observed behaviour, carry only the **host** of
the endpoint, and never a secret.

Without `--api-key-env` or a configuration, the kit reads the conventional variable of the
provider's SDK, declared in `lib/catalog.json`:

| Provider | Variable | Provider | Variable |
|---|---|---|---|
| `openai` | `OPENAI_API_KEY` | `deepseek` | `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY` |
| `anthropic` | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | `kimi` · `moonshot` | `MOONSHOT_API_KEY` |
| `azure` · `azure-openai` | `AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY` | `qwen` | `DASHSCOPE_API_KEY` |
| `mistral` | `MISTRAL_API_KEY` | `minimax` | `MINIMAX_API_KEY` |
| `together` · `togetherai` | `TOGETHER_API_KEY` | `huggingface` · `hf` | `HF_TOKEN` |
| `ollama` | *none* | `zai` · `glm` · `zhipu` | `ZAI_API_KEY` |
| `gemini` · `google` | `GEMINI_API_KEY` | `grok` · `xai` | `XAI_API_KEY` |
| `openrouter` | `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` | `mammouth` | `MAMMOUTH_API_KEY` |

`--api-key-env` wins, then the `apiKeyEnv` field of the configuration, then this table, and
finally `ORKEON_LLM_API_KEY`. The default used to be `ORKEON_LLM_API_KEY` for all thirteen:
any campaign launched without `--config` looked for a variable nobody exports.

### What each provider serves — `lib/served-models.json`

A campaign is also when the list of models is read. `lib/served-models.json` is the dated
snapshot of what each provider's own catalogue endpoint answered to the campaign key —
every identifier, and beside it the options the endpoint publishes for that model: context
and output cap (Anthropic, DeepSeek, Gemini, Mammouth, OpenRouter), default temperature
(Gemini, Mistral), effort levels and their default (Anthropic, DeepSeek, OpenRouter),
modalities and prices (Grok, Together), routed providers (HuggingFace), context and
image / video / reasoning flags (Kimi). Four vendors publish identifiers and nothing else
(OpenAI, Qwen, Z.AI, MiniMax) — and what a model *refuses* is published by none: it is
only known by calling it, and lands in `requiredParams`.

```bash
# The identifiers alone, live:
orkeon llm models -p mistral -k MISTRAL_API_KEY --json
# The snapshot's identifiers (every campaign prints what changed since, at its end):
jq -r '.providers.mistral.models | keys[]' llmproviders-test/lib/served-models.json
```

Nothing reads the snapshot at run time: it is the baseline the next campaign diffs against,
and the source of the *Models served and their default options* section of
`docs/reference/llm-providers-comparison.md`. A model found there and never campaigned is
played once on M1, M5 and M7 in a throwaway `--out` root (`.out-*`, gitignored) to learn
what it refuses, pinned in `requiredParams` accordingly, then run in full — and the full
run still has the last word: Kimi's provider retries a refused temperature on buffered
calls, so `kimi-k2.7-code` passed that pre-pass at 0 and only its streams showed the mandate.

These identifiers come from the §6.x sections of the matrix, **not from the defaults compiled
into the providers**: six of those are flagged there as withdrawn or wrong (G-01 to G-04,
G-07, G-08). Inheriting them would have sent every other campaign to a model the API no
longer serves.

**Gemini is the only exception, and for a reason that will not recur**: it arrived after the
2026-07-27 audit, no §6.x covered it, and its §6.13 sheet was therefore opened from its
compiled default — `gemini-3.7-flash`, verified on 2026-08-18 against Google's OpenAI
compatibility documentation. It is a dated default, not one inherited from a stale
generation; the campaign remains what confirms it.

**Azure declares none, deliberately.** Deployments belong to an account, there is no portable
catalog, and inventing one would send every campaign to a deployment nobody created. Azure
therefore requires `--model <deployment>` or an entry in the JSON — and says so rather than
failing further down.

### The companion vision campaign

When a provider's default model does not see but the provider declares a model that does,
**M9 is replayed on that one**, in addition. This is the practical half of D-03: capabilities
are declared per provider, reality is per model, so a single default model can never answer
for M9 at a provider whose sight lives in another identifier. Measured twice on 2026-08-02 —
`glm-5.2` returns `1210` where `glm-4.6v-flash` reads the image, `llama3.2` refuses
multimodal input where `llava` reads it.

The default model **keeps its M9 and keeps its red**: that red *is* the evidence of D-03, and
removing it would hide precisely the gap the matrix exists to track. The companion adds the
complementary fact — that Orkeon's multimodal path works — which neither gives on its own.

Only on the automatic path: an explicit `--model` is a choice, and contradicting it would
spend credits you did not ask to spend.

## Custom endpoints

The `custom-endpoints/` folder archives the campaigns run against an arbitrary
OpenAI-compatible endpoint through the fallback (`--provider openai --base-url … --out
llmproviders-test/custom-endpoints --no-recap`): they validate the "unknown compatible
server" path without polluting the index of the official providers. First piece of evidence:
`api.x.ai` / `grok-4.6`, 12/12 on 2026-08-30.

## The wildcard

A `--model` containing `*` or `?` triggers
`orkeon llm models -p <provider> --filter <pattern>`, which queries the upstream catalog. If
the call fails — missing endpoint, network, Azure which has no public catalog — the kit falls
back on the `models` list declared for that provider in the JSON, filtered by the same
pattern. The `--max-models` cap then applies, and **what is dropped is logged**: a silent cap
would read as complete coverage.

## The protocol modes

The harness covers **M1 to M10, M12, M13 and M15 to M18** for a chat provider, **D1 to D8** for a decision
provider (below). A `➖` in a report flags a mode the provider
cannot satisfy — nothing was exercised, there is nothing to fix.

### M15 to M17 — reasoning

M7 is the single smoke test of a reasoning effort. Three modes go further, one step each, and every
step is its own row in the report's `Reasoning` section:

- **M15, thinking toggle**: two steps, `on` (thinking enabled) and `off` (thinking disabled).
- **M16, effort sweep**: one step per effort, by default `low, medium, high, xhigh, max`. The catalog
  can replace the list for a model that takes vendor values (`requiredParams.<model>.sweepEfforts`,
  for instance `none,low,…`); `run-campaign` passes it as `--sweep-efforts`, and the report header
  prints it.
- **M17, thinking budget**: one step, `budget` (1024 tokens).

A step ends in one of four outcomes: `✅ sent` (the value went out as asked), `✅ lowered→<value>`
(Orkeon sent the nearest value the model takes), `➖ omitted` (nothing was sent: the model or the
dialect has no such control) or `❌ rejected` (the vendor refused what Orkeon sent). A mode is failed
when one of its steps is rejected, passed when a step was sent or lowered, not applicable otherwise.
The `Reasoning` section also shows the vendor's `wire` value, whether a reasoning trace came back,
the reasoning tokens and the finish reason. The last three are read twice: from what the provider
surfaced, and from the vendor's answer on the wire before the provider parsed it (`vendorTrace`,
`vendorReasoningTokens`, `vendorFinishReason` in the JSON). `Trace` reads `wire only` when the vendor
sent a trace that the provider dropped; tokens and finish show the provider's value, else the
vendor's. Reports of earlier campaigns have no such section, and reports before the vendor read have
no vendor fields.

The `Reasoning per model` table below (also published in the documentation) reads one model per row:
a `✅` cell was sent as asked, `→low` was lowered to `low`, `➖` was left out, `❌` was refused by the
vendor (a vendor refusal of a value Orkeon sent, not a harness failure to run), and an empty cell
means the step was not run. `Other` lists vendor steps (`none ✅`); `Trace` is `✅` when the provider
surfaced a reasoning trace on any step, `wire only` when only the vendor's answer carried one.

### M18 — raw reasoning matrix

M15 to M17 judge what Orkeon sends. M18 asks the vendor instead: for each fragment of a list, the probe
makes one short call through the normal provider, but an HTTP handler strips every reasoning field Orkeon
wrote and deep-merges the fragment into the request body, so the vendor sees exactly that fragment.

- The list is the catalog's `providers.<key>.rawReasoning`, an array of `{ "label": "effort:xhigh",
  "body": { "reasoning_effort": "xhigh" } }` in the provider's own dialect. A model's
  `requiredParams.<model>.rawReasoning` is appended to it (a label already present is replaced by the
  model's item). `run-campaign` resolves the list into a temporary file and passes it as
  `--raw-reasoning`; a provider with no list (Azure, Ollama, the decision providers) reports `➖`.
- Each fragment is a step of the `Reasoning` section, with its `wire` value: `✅ accepted` (the vendor
  answered 2xx) or `❌ refused` (the start of its answer is in the note), the reasoning tokens, the
  completion tokens and whether a trace came back. The mode is passed when at least one fragment was
  accepted, failed when all were refused, not applicable without a list.
- `accepted` is HTTP 2xx and nothing more: a vendor may swallow a field it ignores. Compare the trace
  and the token counts of the steps to see which values had an effect.

The `Vendor reasoning matrix` table below (also published in the documentation) reads one model per row,
from its latest report that ran M18, and lists the accepted, refused and traced labels (a trace the
vendor sent counts, whether or not the provider surfaced it).

### Decision providers — D1 to D8

TypeSafe (Jev), Liquid and Kev are **decision models**: they answer typed questions about a
state, and do not chat, stream or call tools, so no M mode applies to them.
`orkeon llm probe -p typesafe` runs their own modes through `SystemOneDecisionModel`, the
client the framework itself uses, and writes the same JSON, so the kit archives and indexes
them like any other campaign. The catalog gives each one its mode set (`modes`), and the
report says `Temperature: not pinned` because the wire has no sampling parameter.

| Mode | What it checks |
|---|---|
| D1 | A `noul` with instructions and criteria leans yes (≥ 0.5) on an obvious yes, with input tokens counted |
| D2 | A three-option `choice` picks the obvious option, with probabilities that sum to 1 |
| D3 | A three-level `score` lands at 1 or above on an urgent message |
| D4 | A `box` on a 320×320 PNG asset touches where the digits are, and is not the whole image; the IoU is reported, not judged. ➖ on Kev, which takes no box |
| D5 | A state of about 100k tokens is refused as a non-transient 4xx that names the 64k context limit |
| D6 | An invalid model is a typed, non-transient 4xx — never a retry loop |
| D7 | A call cancelled after 50 ms stops |
| D8 | With long context set, the same 100k-token state is answered, its input tokens counted over 64k, and the one sentence asking for a refund, buried halfway, is found. **Paid** (about 100k input tokens a run): in no default set, run only when named. ➖ where the provider serves no long context (only TypeSafe does) |

```bash
export TYPESAFE_API_KEY=…
llmproviders-test/run-campaign.sh --provider typesafe --candidates   # jev-latest, then jev-preview
llmproviders-test/run-campaign.sh --provider typesafe --modes D8       # the long context, paid
```

### M2 and its two shapes

**M2 sends the conversation twice** (two billed calls instead of one), and that is
deliberate. OpenAI-compatible providers have two chat paths, chosen on a criterion the caller
does not see: with no tool declared, the conversation is **flattened** into a single user turn
(`"user: …\nassistant: …"`); with a tool, it leaves as a **real `messages` array**. Exercising
only one of the two forms let a real defect through (D-02: system message lost on the native
path alone). The two forms also produce a verdict that either alone cannot give:

| Flattened | `messages` array | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| ✅ | ✅ | Nothing to report |
| ❌ | ✅ | **Orkeon defect** — the flattening is what lost the model |
| ✅ | ❌ | Inspect the payload of the structured path, **but do not conclude too fast** (see below) |
| ❌ | ❌ | The instruction did reach the API both ways: **the model does not follow it** |

> ⚠️ **What the third row does not prove.** The structured path is only reachable by sending
> a tool schema — that is what selects it. Two things therefore change together: the shape of
> the request *and* the presence of a tool catalog in the context, the latter being enough to
> degrade instruction-following in some models. The probe emits `tool_choice: "none"` to at
> least rule out the "the model called the tool instead of answering" case, but it cannot
> isolate the rest. A `✅ / ❌` calls for a reading of the emitted payload, not an immediate fix.
>
> **Measured on 2026-08-01, and investigated to the end.** At the framework's default
> temperature (`0.7`), three runs of M2 alone on the same `llama3.2` returned ❌ ✅ ❌ — a
> verdict decided by a coin toss. At `temperature: 0`, all three return ❌, still on the
> structured form. The payload inspection this row calls for was done and **pinned in a test**
> (`OllamaChatEndpointTests.ShouldCarryTheConfiguredSystemMessage_OnTheStructuredPath`):
> Ollama builds its own `/api/chat` payload and correctly prepends the system message. The
> instruction does reach the model, which does not follow it as soon as a tool catalog shares
> its context. **Model behaviour, not an Orkeon defect** — but it is the test that says so,
> not a code reading done once.

## Reproducibility — the temperature

The probe pins **`temperature: 0`** on every call. This is a fix, not a preference: the
harness inherited the framework default (`0.7`) and was therefore measuring conformance
through creative sampling — hence the ❌ ✅ ❌ above. Every report now carries the value used;
a report marked `non épinglée` ("not pinned") predates this fix and its verdict must be read
as indicative.

Two limits worth knowing, rather than discovering them mid-campaign:

- **Determinism stays approximate.** `LlmConfig.Seed` exists but **no HTTP provider puts it on
  the wire** — only the Microsoft.Extensions.AI adapters read it. The probe therefore does not
  set it: writing a field that goes nowhere would be exactly the *silent drop* this project
  fights. At `temperature: 0` the variance becomes small, not null.
- **A few models refuse any imposed temperature** and accept only their own default. The
  refusal is explicit on the provider side, not silent — but it applies to *every* call, so it
  does not colour one mode, it takes down twelve. The Kimi campaign of 2026-08-03 paid full
  price: `kimi-k2.6` answers `invalid temperature: only 1 is allowed for this model`, ten modes
  out of twelve red, one single cause. This page already documented it — with nothing applying
  it. Since then, **a provider that does not support `0` declares its temperature in the
  catalog** (`lib/catalog.json`, `temperature` field), `--temperature` still wins, and the
  report header carries the value actually used: a Kimi verdict is not reproducible in the
  same way as a zero-temperature verdict, and that can be read.

A mode that stays unstable at zero temperature reflects a model sitting on a decision
boundary. Running it three times and reporting the trend is worth more than archiving one
pass.

**M11 (long context) and M14 (end-to-end crew) stay manual**, and that is deliberate:

- **M11** bills a request close to the advertised window — up to 1M tokens on GPT-5.6 or
  Claude. The matrix documents two traps it must settle by measurement: native context ≠
  served context, and some providers count input + output together. Procedure: build a prompt
  of the target size, call, check for the absence of silent truncation, record the measured
  value on the **path actually taken**.
- **M14** requires a real crew with delegation. Go through an example from the `examples/`
  folder configured on the target provider, and archive its output.

## Budget

Prefer the cheapest model of each family for M1–M6, and reserve the high end for the modes
that require it (M7 thinking, M9 vision, M11 long context). Frame the budget per provider
**before** launching: these campaigns consume real credits on real accounts.

## Reporting into the matrix

Every report ends with the two ready-to-paste fragments: the §7 journal row and the §6 model
table row. Filling the matrix (LLM-08/C4) is mechanical.

## Reasoning per model

One row per model that ran the reasoning modes (M15 thinking toggle, M16 effort sweep, M17 budget),
from the model's latest campaign day. A cell is ✅ when the value was sent as asked, `→low` when
Orkeon lowered it to the nearest value the model takes, ➖ when it was left out, ❌ when the vendor
refused what Orkeon sent, and empty when the step was not run. `Other` lists vendor values outside
the usual set (`none ✅`); `Trace` is ✅ when the provider surfaced a reasoning trace, `wire only` when the vendor sent one the provider dropped.

## Vendor reasoning matrix

M18 sends each fragment of the catalog's `rawReasoning` list to the vendor exactly as written,
bypassing Orkeon's own judgement of what a model supports: the table shows what the vendor itself
accepts, from the model's latest report that ran M18. "Accepted" means HTTP 2xx, not that the value
had an effect: compare the traces and the completion tokens in the reports. `Trace` lists the
fragments after which the vendor answer carried a reasoning trace, read on the wire.
